objective: Configure a shared directory with group ownership, the setgid bit and the sticky bit
secondaryObjectives: Create and manage users and groups with useradd, usermod, groupadd and passwd
Read and set permissions with chmod in symbolic and octal form, and ownership with chown

sources.cite: inode(7), file mode bits: set-group-ID and sticky bit (man7.org, man-pages 6.19)
sources.note: Relevant text: 'For newly created files, the file group ID is either the group ID of the parent directory or the effective group ID of the creating process, depending on whether or not the set-group-ID bit is set on the parent directory'; 'The sticky bit (S_ISVTX) on a directory means that a file in that directory can be renamed or deleted only by the owner of the file, by the owner of the directory, and by a privileged process.' Read in full 2026-11-14.

Relevant text: -G, --groups: 'If the user is currently a member of a group which is not listed, the user will be removed from the group. This behaviour can be changed via the -a option, which appends the user to the current supplementary group list.' Read in full 2026-11-14.

Relevant text: ps format specifier supgrp, 'group names of supplementary groups, if any'; newgrp(1): 'The newgrp command is used to change the current group ID during a login session.' A running process keeps the supplementary groups it started with, so a group added with usermod reaches a user at the next login (the standard credentials model; credentials(7) read 2026-11-14). Read in full 2026-11-14.

Relevant text: octal modes, the setgid and sticky bits, and 'For directories chmod preserves set-user-ID and set-group-ID bits unless you explicitly specify otherwise.' Read in full 2026-11-14. Command output layouts are authored in each tool's style.

brief.situation: You are the Linux admin at Puyallup Print Co-op (fictional). Yesterday nora joined the print team and was added to the group print with usermod -aG print nora. Today she cannot save into the team folder /srv/jobs, and nobody can edit the jobs omar and jin dropped there this morning. The 11:00 print run needs everyone's files in place. Fix it so the team can share the folder properly, without opening it to everyone.
handover: /srv/jobs is owned by root, group print, mode 0775.
nora has been logged in since before she was added to print.
howItWorks: Run commands from the command line: type one, or pick it from the suggestions or the action list. Only this lab's commands run; there is no free shell, and each command's arguments are fixed.
Each command takes operator time: run it, then let it finish, which moves the clock by the minutes it takes. The outage keeps developing on the same clock.
The map shows each host, disk or service and the links between them, with a status in words. Output appears in the terminal as it happens.
When you declare the service restored, you write the incident record and explain your reasoning.

source.note: How many operator minutes each command takes, and when the fictional outage spreads, are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values. The print run starts at 11:00, 40 minutes after the start.

writeup.question: For the ticket: why nora was denied although id showed her in print, why nobody could edit the morning's jobs, and why your settings will keep working for the next new file.

parts.label: Cause
parts.criteria: Two causes: her login session started before she joined print (a process keeps the groups it started with; id nora reads the group database, not her session), and the existing files carried each author's own group with 644, because the folder had no setgid.
parts.modelAnswer: id nora reads /etc/group, which already listed print, but her shell started before the change, and ps showed its groups without print. Separately, omar's and jin's files were group omar and jin, mode 644, because without setgid a new file takes its creator's group.

parts.label: Evidence
parts.criteria: Uses ps supgrp (or the session's id) and ls -l before changing anything; does not assume a disk or SELinux problem.
parts.modelAnswer: ps -o supgrp -u nora showed nora,design; ls -l showed the files' groups and 644.

parts.label: Fix
parts.criteria: New login for nora (or newgrp), chgrp -R print and g+w on the existing files, g+s on the folder so new files inherit print (sticky optional, to stop deleting others' files); never 777 and never usermod -G without -a.
parts.modelAnswer: nora logged in again; chgrp -R print and chmod -R g+w fixed the existing jobs; chmod g+s makes every new file group print, and +t stops members deleting each other's files. 777 would let every account change the jobs; usermod -G without -a removes her other groups.

fixed.headline: Good: shared properly
fixed.body: You saw that a session keeps the groups it started with and that the folder lacked setgid, fixed both, and proved it with a new file.

fixedGaps.headline: Working, with gaps
fixedGaps.body: The team can share. The criteria show what it cost: time, a change before the evidence, no setgid for the next file, or no check.

openedUp.headline: Opened to everyone
openedUp.body: 777 makes the symptom go away for every account on the host, not only the team. Group ownership, group write and setgid do the job.

lockedOut.headline: Groups replaced
lockedOut.body: usermod -G sets the whole supplementary list; -aG appends. nora was already in print; she only needed a new login.

runMissed.headline: The print run went without the jobs
runMissed.body: ps and ls -l show both causes in two minutes; the fix is a login and three commands.

stillBroken.headline: Closed too soon
stillBroken.body: Check with a new file as nora before closing.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No record was written before the run's hard limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: id nora reads the group database, but a running session keeps the groups it started with, so nora needs a new login (or newgrp). The existing files took their authors' groups because /srv/jobs had no setgid: chgrp -R print and chmod -R g+w fix them, chmod g+s keeps new files in print, and +t stops members deleting each other's work. Never 777, never usermod -G without -a.
